title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers deployed deepfake and voice-cloning technology to impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney, in order to defraud victims. The system operated on social media and through phone calls, targeting immigrants and others seeking legal services or claiming family emergencies. The failure was fundamental: there was no verification that the person on the call or in the message was who they claimed to be, and the technology made such verification harder for victims to perform themselves.

The scam worked because generative AI lowered the cost of impersonation below what human judgment alone could easily detect. Criminals extracted voice samples from social media videos and cloned them convincingly enough to fool people under time pressure or emotional distress. A detection system would have required either the victims themselves to have ways to verify identity independently, or the platforms and communication channels carrying these frauds to check whether the person initiating contact was genuine before allowing the interaction to proceed.

It is not established whether the AI systems themselves were purpose-built for fraud or were commercial tools repurposed by criminals for it.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit fraud across Georgia and South Florida by creating deepfakes of voices, photos, and phone calls to impersonate trusted individuals. A South Florida immigration attorney discovered criminals had cloned his voice to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year, with Florida reporting 350 complaints resulting in $39.9 million in losses and Georgia reporting 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million in losses.

Criminals use generative AI to make traditional scams more convincing by cloning voices from social media videos, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching family relationships. The grandparent scam has become particularly effective with voice-cloning technology, where fraudsters call victims claiming a relative needs emergency money. Financial institutions warn customers that AI makes impersonation attempts harder to detect. Authorities recommend establishing code words with family members, verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, and avoiding immediate money transfers based on phone calls or emails.
